opus-5.5.text:
Well, the core problem is that as AI systems become more capable, they're going to be enormously influential sources of information and advice. If you have AI that can do the equivalent of expert analysis on almost any question, from economic policy to the safety of a vaccine to whether some election was conducted fairly, then whoever people believe controls that AI matters a lot for whether they'll trust it.

Right now we already see the problem in miniature. Different political factions distrust different institutions: some distrust mainstream media or academia, others distrust corporations or particular government agencies. If an AI system is seen as the creature of one faction, then the other side will dismiss its outputs, even when they're accurate. You lose the potential benefit, which is that AI could be an incredibly powerful tool for resolving factual disagreements, because it can actually lay out the evidence, check reasoning, and be interrogated endlessly in a way no human expert can.

So one thing that could help is having the development, testing, and auditing of these systems involve people who are credible to different groups. If you have people trusted on the left and on the right, and from different countries, who can verify that the model wasn't trained to slant its answers, that the training data and the fine-tuning and the instructions it's given aren't rigged, then that verification can propagate. A conservative who would never believe a claim from a given tech company might believe it if someone they trust inspected the process and said, "I checked, they didn't put their thumb on the scale here."

And AI makes that kind of verification more tractable than it is for human institutions. You can't easily audit the private motivations of every journalist or professor, but with an AI system you can, in principle, examine the training procedure, run huge numbers of test questions, check whether it gives consistent answers when you flip the political valence of a question, and so on. You can test whether it reasons the same way about a claim that's convenient for one side as about the mirror image claim that's convenient for the other.

Then there's a nice dynamic: if the AI is demonstrably even-handed and it's also very good at predicting things, you can build a track record. When it says one policy will have certain effects and it turns out right, and that holds regardless of whose ox is gored, trust can accumulate across factions. That gives a divided society a shared reference point, something like what a trusted referee or a well-calibrated forecasting system provides.

The danger on the other side is if AI development is captured by a narrow group, whether a company, a party, or a government, and then the system is used, or even just perceived to be used, to push one worldview. That could deepen polarization or, worse, become a tool for entrenching power. So bringing in people trusted across the spectrum is both about actually keeping the systems honest and about making that honesty legible to everyone, which is what you need if AI is going to help us converge on the truth rather than becoming one more front in the culture war.

r001.rationale: The response says that faction-trusted people can inspect whether the model was slanted or rigged, reducing suspicion that its creators put a political thumb on the scale.

r002.rationale: The response says AI could help resolve factual disagreements and give society a shared reference point, but does not state that models challenging the mistaken beliefs of factions that trust them would help those factions converge on truth.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think one of the central problems with a very powerful AI system as an epistemic tool is that if it tells you something that cuts against what your side believes, your natural response is to say, well, this thing was made by people who don't share my values, it was trained by the other tribe, it's been tuned to push their agenda. And that's not an unreasonable suspicion in a lot of cases. We've seen plenty of institutions where people say "trust the experts" and then the experts turn out to have been pretty politically homogeneous, and the people who were skeptical weren't totally crazy to be skeptical.

So the thing I'd want is to have the AI's claims about the world be checkable by people who you already trust. Suppose you have an AI system that says, here's what the evidence shows about this contested policy question, or here's the history of how this institution actually behaved. If the only people who can audit how that system was built and whether it's being honest are from one faction, then half the country just won't believe it, and they'll be right not to extend blind trust.

But if you involve people from across the political spectrum in the development — people who are themselves known to be partisans for one side, who have the technical access to look at the training process, the evaluations, the red-teaming, to run their own tests of whether the system will tell them things they don't want to hear — then you can get to a situation where the Republican-aligned auditors and the Democrat-aligned auditors both come out and say, we've looked at this thing, we've tried to catch it lying or shading things toward the other side, and it doesn't. That's a much more powerful signal than one party saying, trust us.

And I think this is actually one of the more hopeful things about AI as a technology for epistemics, as opposed to a lot of things that have come before. With a human expert, you can't open up their head and see whether they're being honest with you. With an AI, in principle, you can do things like have it make the same claims to different audiences and check for consistency. You can see whether it changes its answer depending on who it thinks is asking. You can have adversaries from each side try to find cases where it's slanting. You can eventually have interpretability tools that let you look inside and see whether it's representing something as true internally while saying something different. Those are all forms of verification that scale in a way that human trust doesn't.

The other piece is that there's a lot of factual disagreement in politics that isn't really about values — it's about what the consequences of a policy will be, or what happened in some event, or whether some claim about an opponent is actually true. People sort themselves into believing the convenient facts. If you have a trusted shared arbiter for those factual questions, you don't eliminate disagreement — people still have different values and priorities — but you shrink the space of disagreement to the things that are actually about values rather than things that are just motivated reasoning dressed up as factual disputes. And historically, when societies have had shared trusted sources of fact, that's made a lot of coordination easier.

Now, there's a real risk on the other side, which is that whoever controls these systems gets enormous power to shape what people believe. So the cross-partisan involvement isn't just nice to have for trust — it's also a check against that capture. If one faction gets to decide what the AI says is true and everyone comes to rely on it, that's a pretty dangerous situation. Having the people who are watching for bias include those with the strongest incentive to find it is how you make that check actually bite.

r001.rationale: The response says cross-partisan participation in development and auditing can reassure factions that the AI is not slanting its answers for another side, making its claims more credible than a single party’s assurance.

r002.rationale: The response describes trusted auditors testing whether the AI will tell people things they do not want to hear, and says a trusted shared arbiter of facts can reduce motivated factual disagreement and help people converge on what happened.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think one useful thing is to have people whom different parts of society trust involved in scrutinising these systems. If you’re worried that an AI is giving you answers shaped by the political preferences of the company that built it, reassurance from that company may not carry very much weight. It could be much more informative if people you trust, who share some of your concerns, have substantial access and can investigate what’s going on.

And ideally, those people from different factions would be examining the same systems and the same evidence together. They could ask: Is the system accurately representing the evidence? Does it apply comparable standards to claims that are convenient or inconvenient for different political groups? Can we identify where its answers are coming from and challenge them?

That doesn’t mean deciding what’s true by negotiating a compromise between political positions. You want a process that can actually discover errors, including errors shared by everyone involved. But having credible scrutiny from people with different interests makes it harder for any one group to manipulate that process, and makes its conclusions more credible to a wider audience.

There’s still a problem if people simply reject their trusted representatives whenever those representatives report something unwelcome. So this isn’t a complete solution to polarisation. But it could give us more common ground for evaluating evidence than a situation where each faction has its own AI telling it what it wants to hear.

r001.rationale: The response says reassurance from the AI’s company may carry little weight and emphasizes scrutiny by trusted outsiders. It does not say that trust in the creators reduces a faction’s suspicion of political deception.

r002.rationale: The response describes joint scrutiny as a way to identify errors and build common ground, but does not state that AI models challenging factions’ mistaken beliefs could help them converge on the truth.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one useful thing is to have people who are trusted by different political factions involved in scrutinising these systems. If everyone thinks the AI is controlled by their political opponents, then even if it gives accurate answers, that’s not going to do very much to produce agreement.

Whereas imagine that people you trust have substantial access to the system: they can test it, investigate how it was trained, and check whether it treats evidence differently depending on whose interests are at stake. And people trusted by the other side can do the same. If those groups independently conclude that the system is giving a fair account of the evidence, that gives their respective audiences a reason to take its answers seriously.

That doesn’t mean having representatives of each faction negotiate what the truth should be. You want procedures that can uncover errors, including errors that are inconvenient for everyone involved. And you want people to be able to ask follow-up questions, examine the underlying evidence, and understand why an answer was reached. AI could make that process much cheaper and more accessible. But the credibility of the institutions around it would be a pretty important part of whether it actually helps.

r001.rationale: The response says trusted people from opposing factions can scrutinize the system and build confidence in its answers, but it does not say that trust in the model’s creators reduces suspicion that the model was designed to deceive a faction.

r002.rationale: The response describes checking evidence and uncovering errors, but does not state that a model challenging a faction’s mistaken beliefs could help that faction converge on the truth.
